Laboratory colonies of Trumpet ramshorn (Dilatata dilatata) maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] provide detailed insight into the species' early life history. Freshly deposited egg masses hatch after an incubation period of approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], yielding offspring with a remarkably small total length at birth of just 0.038 cm [ at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]Lb = 0.038 cm]. These minute neonates, barely visible to the unaided eye, immediately commence grazing on periphytic biofilm. The rapid development of the veliger and early post-metamorphic juvenile stages is strongly temperature-dependent; at the standard rearing temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the transition from yolk-dependent embryo to exogenously feeding juvenile proceeds without a prolonged planktonic phase. This compressed developmental timeline is consistent with observations in other planorbid species inhabiting shallow, ephemeral water bodies where rapid maturation confers a distinct selective advantage.

Juvenile Dilatata dilatata undergo a period of accelerated growth following the onset of exogenous feeding, gradually approaching their asymptotic body dimensions. The ultimate total length attained by fully grown adults is approximately 0.9 cm [Li = approximately 0.9 cm], a modest shell size that aligns with the species' occupation of vegetated microhabitats in slow-moving freshwater systems. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight recorded for reproductively mature individuals is 0.53 g [Wwi = 0.53 g], a value derived from size-corrected allometric relationships within the Planorbidae. This adult body mass is considerably lower than that of the related Planorbarius corneus, reflecting the more diminutive shell dimensions of Dilatata dilatata. Shell growth decelerates markedly as individuals approach this asymptotic size, with energy increasingly directed toward gonadal development and reproductive functions rather than somatic expansion.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs well before the attainment of maximum shell dimensions, a common life-history pattern among freshwater gastropods. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonad maturation and gametogenesis, is reached when individuals achieve a total length of 0.18 cm [Lp = 0.18 cm], based on growth trajectory data indicating an age at puberty of approximately 50 days post-hatching. This size threshold represents roughly twenty percent of the ultimate adult length, suggesting that reproductive activation is initiated relatively early in the growth trajectory. The transition from immature post-metamorphic juvenile to reproductively viable adult is accompanied by pronounced morphological changes, including the differentiation of the reproductive tract and the development of the copulatory apparatus. Individuals at this stage become capable of both receiving and transferring sperm during reproductive pairing.

Under the controlled thermal conditions described previously (25 °C [T = 25 °C]), reproductively active adults exhibit a well-defined reproductive schedule. The maximum reproductive rate observed in laboratory settings is one egg mass every four days [Ri = one egg mass every four days], with each mass typically containing a modest complement of developing embryos. This rate of reproductive activity is sustained throughout the peak breeding season and is contingent on consistent food availability in the form of algal detritus and microbial biofilm. Females that are gravid can be identified by the translucent appearance of the shell apex, through which the developing embryos are visible. The species engages in reciprocal copulation prior to each round of egg mass deposition.

Longevity records from captive populations maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of 150 days [am = 150 days], a relatively short duration that places Dilatata dilatata among the faster-lived planorbid gastropods. This abbreviated life history — with hatching at 6 days [ab = 6 days], adults reaching only 0.9 cm [Li = 0.9 cm] in shell length, and an asymptotic body mass of 0.53 g [Wwi = 0.53 g] — is typical of a rapid turnover strategy at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The onset of reproductive activity at a shell length of 0.18 cm [Lp = 0.18 cm] ensures early population replenishment. Natural mortality in the wild likely truncates this laboratory lifespan considerably, with predation from leeches, aquatic insects, and small fishes representing the primary sources of extrinsic mortality.
